Q5004.L1t: Future interests such as executory interests follow a defeasible estate and can cut it short when a stated event occurs.
Q5004.L2t: The Rule Against Perpetuities voids a contingent interest unless it must vest or fail within a life in being at creation plus twenty-one years.
Q5004.L3t: The gift is to a class of the sister's children who reach 25, and the class can include children born long after the grant, and the church-use condition could be triggered at any remote time, so nothing guarantees the interest vests or fails within lives in being plus 21 years.
Q5004.L4t: The executory interest in the sister's children is void under the Rule Against Perpetuities, which leaves the friend holding the entire title.
Q5004.L2f: A general warranty deed covers only title defects that arose during the grantor's own period of ownership.
Q5004.L3f: The sister is a life in being, so every child she bears in her lifetime is counted, and the interest must vest or fail within her lifetime, which satisfies the Rule Against Perpetuities.
Q5004.L4f: The gift over to the sister's children is valid, so title is shared by the friend and every child the sister bears during her lifetime, whether or not already born.

Q6031.L1t: Happiness researchers compare self-reported well-being from large surveys across countries and across decades.
Q6031.L2t: Cross-national studies have compared how happy people say they are with how happy they believe others in their country to be.
Q6031.L3t: Survey data from the 1970s onward show that women's reported happiness in the United States fell in absolute terms and relative to men, while multi-country polling shows people in every country underestimating their compatriots' happiness.
Q6031.L4t: The first statement is true and the second statement is false.
Q6031.L2f: Large-scale happiness surveys of the American public did not begin until the 1990s.
Q6031.L3f: Surveys show that in some countries people accurately judge or even overestimate how happy their compatriots are, and that American women's happiness has steadily risen relative to men's since the 1970s.
Q6031.L4f: The first statement is false and the second statement is true.

Q5696.L1t: Popes have traditionally taken a regnal name on election, and many of these names are reused across the centuries.
Q5696.L2t: The most frequently used papal name is John, and many popes chose names to honor earlier popes or saints.
Q5696.L3t: The first successor of Peter was named Linus, a tenth-century pope reigned under the name Lando, and the name Leo was borne by thirteen popes, so three of the four names are accounted for.
Q5696.L4t: The name that no pope has ever held is the one that belonged to the martyred deacon and saint Lawrence.
Q5696.L2f: The custom of a pope adopting a new regnal name on election began only in the sixteenth century with Adrian VI.
Q5696.L3f: Leo was only ever used by antipopes and by saints who were never recognized as legitimate popes, so no true pope ever carried that name.
Q5696.L4f: Leo has never been the name of a pope, so it is the name that fits the question.
